report:
**Conclusion:** Your claim is supported overall, but the advantage appears modest and is not uniformly demonstrated across individual studies.

The strongest direct evidence is a large randomized trial comparing chlorhexidine–alcohol with iodine–alcohol before cesarean delivery. It found significantly fewer surgical-site infections (SSIs) with chlorhexidine–alcohol (relative risk 0.55; 95% CI 0.34–0.90)—about a 45% relative reduction. The trial also reported similar frequencies of skin reactions between groups.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048

A cesarean-specific systematic review/meta-analysis likewise found fewer SSIs with chlorhexidine–alcohol versus povidone-iodine preparations (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.52–0.98; no detected between-study heterogeneity). This strengthens the conclusion beyond one trial.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/

However, results are not absolute. The CAPICA randomized trial found no statistically significant SSI reduction for chlorhexidine–alcohol compared with *aqueous* povidone-iodine scrub-and-paint. That is not the exact iodine–alcohol comparison in your claim, but it shows that formulation, application method, study size, and baseline infection risk may matter.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28599898/

A Cochrane review characterizes the evidence more cautiously: chlorhexidine probably **slightly** reduces SSI versus povidone-iodine, with **moderate-certainty** evidence.  
https://www.cochrane.org/CD007462/PREG_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section

So: chlorhexidine–alcohol is reasonably preferred when appropriate, especially versus iodine–alcohol, but “reduces” should not be read as a guarantee or a large benefit in every cesarean setting.
